To validate the utility of the computer vision (CV)-derived metrics and assess their alignment with established gameplay standards, we compare them against aggregate performance statistics obtained through Riot's public API. The Riot API provides large-scale, ranked match data that serves as a population-level benchmark for farming-related indicators such as CS@10 and gold accumulation across tiers. In contrast, the video-derived data allows for more granular evaluation at the individual player level, including temporal skill execution patterns and minion-type specificity, which are not captured by the API.

Our comparison strategy involves aligning both data sources at common time anchors (e.g., 10-minute marks) and normalizing for factors such as role, champion matchup, and player tier. Where available, we compute summary statistics from API data (mean, standard deviation) to establish expected value ranges for each tier. CV-derived metrics, such as CS@10, gold deviation, and wave efficiency, are then mapped onto these benchmarks using z-scores and percentile ranks to evaluate whether a player over-or underperforms relative to their peer group. Although the Riot API lacks detailed minion-type or skill usage breakdowns, its breadth enables statistical grounding for the evaluation of farming efficiency, while the CV-derived data contributes depth by revealing how players achieve their outcomes. The integration of these two perspectives supports a comprehensive and ecologically valid analysis of cognitive performance in Esports gameplay.

div.head: | YOLOv8 Trained Model Validation
div.p: To ensure the accuracy and robustness of our computer vision-based gameplay analysis, we implemented a comprehensive validation protocol with manually annotated images to train and validate the YOLOv8 model for champion state detection. The purpose of this protocol is to check whether the trained models are reliable and can be applied to further study, and also to explore the feasibility of using advanced object detection models like YOLOv8 for champion and skill-state recognition. Figure 5 illustrates our annotation environment, highlighting the polygon labelling structure, label tag assignments, and automated detection of static UI components such as skill cooldowns and resource counters.
We established a ground truth dataset through frame-by-frame manual annotation using labelme as CVAT (Computer Vision Annotation Tool). The validation dataset contains:
■ 8,735 frames sampled from 120 matches (20 frames/match) ■ 300 manually annotated champion instances.
■ 2,100 bounding boxes with champion skill annotations and GUI element annotations (gold, timers, skills)

The manually annotated images have been used for training YOLOv8 model for champion skill status tracking, combined with the automatically labelled content to provide more precise information on cooldown time and skill usage status. With the trained model, we manually checked the result of champion state detection from the model and compared it with our manually annotated frames. The result shows that, due to the dynamic nature of champion appearance under different skills, status and skins, the trained YOLOv8 model cannot accurately identify champion movement and skill usage status (identification rate lower than 25%). Despite an extensive annotation effort and the initial deployment of YOLOv8 for champion-state tracking, results revealed significant limitations in reliability and precision.

The YOLOv8 model need to be separately trained for each combination of champion and skin of it as there are large difference in appearance of different skins as shown by 6, which requires thousands of time training, caused prohibitively high cost of training while the model may not be reliable as the appearance of champions might change with update of the LoL game while the in-game appearance will also be largely changes by opponents and friend champion's skills. In LoL gameplay video, the same champion can appear drastically different depending on selected skins and surrounding in-game effects, rendering static model training impractical for reliable cross-champion inference. In contrast, optical character recognition (OCR)-based analysis of the UI proved to be significantly more stable and generalizable. This led us to adopt an OCR-based pipeline for cooldown status and skill activity recognition, which offers high reliability, model reusability, and future-proofing across game patches and champion reworks. Due to the reason above, we decided to use the OCR detection method to identify skill status with cooldown time of skills, which is more general and robust, and can be applied to all champions with high accuracy.

div.head: | Research Question Operationalization and Evaluation Plan
div.p: To operationalize and evaluate the three primary research questions outlined previously, this study implements a mixed-methods approach combining large-scale Riot API statistics with detailed behavioral metrics derived from a custom computer vision analysis pipeline. Each research question corresponds directly to a specific hypothesis, which guides the operational definition of variables, the selection of data sources, and the analytical techniques employed.

To address Research Question 1 (RQ1), which investigates whether performance differences in minion farming manifest across different player skill tiers, we formulate Hypothesis 1 (H1): Players at higher skill tiers (Platinum-Diamond) demonstrate significantly greater early-game farming efficiency compared to players at lower skill tiers (Iron-Gold), as reflected by higher creep scores (CS@10) within the first 10 minutes of gameplay. To evaluate this hypothesis, we extracted ranked match data from Riot's official API across a wide range of skill tiers (Iron to Diamond). The primary metric analyzed was average creep score (CS) at the 10-minute mark, a widely accepted benchmark for early-game performance. The analysis included statistical comparisons across tiers using descriptive statistics, tier-based visualizations, and distribution comparisons to identify systematic differences in farming outcomes. This approach provided a structured and scalable method for validating performance patterns linked to player expertise levels.

The second research question (RQ2) examines how cognitive strategies differ between players using melee and ranged champions in the top lane. To concretize this inquiry, we propose Hypothesis 2 (H2): Players using ranged champions exhibit more efficient attentional resource allocation and lower cognitive load during minion farming tasks compared to players using melee champions, reflected through metrics such as higher Skill Execution Ratio (SER), more stable creep score trajectories, and optimized minion-type prioritization. To evaluate this hypothesis, gameplay videos from controlled experimental matches involving four specific matchup scenarios-Melee vs Melee (MM), Melee vs Ranged (MR), Ranged vs Melee (RM), and Ranged vs Ranged (RR)-are analyzed using the developed computer vision toolkit. Extracted metrics include moment-to-moment CS timelines, skill activation frequencies, wave-based gold efficiency, and inferred distributions of minion types farmed. Analytical approaches involve both quantitative comparisons and qualitative interpretation of player behavior, enabling a detailed examination of cognitive differences induced by champion types.

The third research question (RQ3) addresses the methodological validity and applicability of the computer vision-derived metrics by asking how effectively these metrics align with established Riot Games API performance benchmarks. Accordingly, Hypothesis 3 (H3) states: Behavioral metrics derived from computer vision analysis of gameplay videos-such as creep score per minute, skill usage patterns, and inferred gold trajectories-will show strong positive correlations with official Riot API benchmarks like CS@10 and gold differentials across corresponding skill tiers and champion matchups. To test this hypothesis, a direct correlation analysis between video-derived metrics and Riot API benchmarks is conducted using Pearson correlation coefficients. This evaluation assesses the convergent validity of the computer vision tool by examining statistical alignment, reliability, and consistency across multiple matchups and skill-level datasets.

Together, these three hypotheses structure a robust evaluation framework, explicitly tying the research questions to clearly defined cognitive and behavioral measures. The mixed-methods design ensures each hypothesis is assessed with appropriate analytical rigor, leveraging both macro-level statistics from large-scale API datasets and micro-level behavioral metrics from detailed video analysis. This structured approach provides a comprehensive validation pathway, linking theoretical insights about cognitive processes directly to observable performance outcomes in competitive League of Legends gameplay.

div.head: This section presents both the technical validation of our computer vision (CV)-based analysis toolkit and the empirical findings aligned with the three research questions (RQ1-RQ3).
div.p: For RQ1, we analyze Riot API data to assess whether early-game minion farming efficiency (CS@10) varies across skill tiers, providing a performance baseline across ranked levels. For RQ2, we apply CV-derived metrics to evaluate how champion type influences farming strategies in four controlled matchup scenarios, focusing on skill usage and attentional behavior. For RQ3, we validate the CV-derived indicators against official API benchmarks to assess their reliability as proxies for in-game performance.
Together, these analyses demonstrate how structured metrics extracted from gameplay footage and API data can reveal performance differences shaped by skill, role, and cognitive strategy.

The final two subsections present implementation-level results: the fourth reports on the technical feasibility of the CV pipeline (e.g., OCR accuracy, resolution robustness), and the fifth evaluates performance characterization using manual annotations and benchmarking. These validations reinforce the system's reliability and ensure that its insights can be trusted in both academic and applied settings.

Across all findings, players demonstrating higher cognitive efficiency exhibit stronger creep score consistency, higher wave efficiency, and more effective skill deployment. These patterns reinforce the use of CV-based indicators not only as proxies for raw gameplay metrics but also as interpretable markers of cognitive capacity, particularly attention control, decision timing, and multitasking performance, under dynamic, competitive pressure.

div.head: | Comparative Analysis of Minion Farming Efficiency Across Skill Tiers
div.p: To address Research Question 1 (RQ1), we examined large-scale data from Riot Games' public API, focusing on average creep score (CS), which is a core early-game farming metric. The goal was to determine whether player skill tier correlates with laning efficiency, thereby testing Hypothesis 1 (H1).
CS data were extracted across seven ranked tiers of Iron, Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum, Emerald, and Diamond based on the top lane matchups data we get from the Riot Developer API.

div.head: | Distribution of Minion Farming among Tiers
div.p: The Riot API provided ground truth benchmarks for CS@10 from minion farming at different skill tiers.

The extracted average values from the API datasets are summarized in Table 8. While there is a visible upward trend in Table 8, the differences between adjacent tiers are modest, ranging from 57.25 CS in Iron to 67.99 CS in Diamond. A similar trend is observed in minion farming as shown by Figure 7, though it plateaus beyond Platinum.

Total CS and Gold Accumulation: As illustrated in Table 9, intermediate-tier players demonstrated higher average total CS compared to beginner-tier players. This suggests more effective minion farming strategies and resource management at higher skill levels. However, when comparing the total number of minions farmed (CS) from minion farming, high-tier players show a slightly smaller number compared to intermediate-tier players. That might come from the higher intensity fights and resource management of the later stage (post 10 minutes) for higher-ranked games, which makes players focus more on other strategic moves like team fights. While Table 8 illustrates the average CS at 10 minutes per tier and there is an upward trend is observed, with players in higher skill brackets achieving better minion farming performance. This also implies that within the early stage (first 10 minutes) of the game, all tiers of players are focusing on the minion farming instead of other tasks like team fights. Despite expectations of more significant performance gaps, the distributions of CS per minute across tiers and the accumulated farmed gold reveal only incremental improvements. Figure 7 shows overlapping distributions with some widening at higher tiers, but the median values remain relatively consistent across ranks. This likely reflects the upper bound on minion availability in the early game, which caps performance for even expert players.

div.head: | Visualization of Minion Farming Performance
div.p: A broader comparison of full-match CS in Table 9 also shows relatively small differences between intermediate and high-tier players, with intermediate players slightly outperforming Diamond-tier players on average. One interpretation is that higher-tier games involve greater macro-complexity, such as team fighting, objective control, and roaming, which may reduce farming opportunities in favor of broader strategic impact. Similarly, Figure 8 shows the number of farmed minions (creep score) growth within the first 10-minute mark by tier. While cs scores show a slight plateau beyond Gold rank, the trend generally supports the hypothesis that higher-tier players manage lane resources more efficiently.

Diamond and higher-ranked players consistently farm more minions earlier and at a faster rate compared to lower-ranked players. The gap widens progressively from 5 to 10 minutes, reflecting better early-game laning and farming strategies. Efficient early minion farming is crucial for reaching item power spikes sooner, contributing to strategic advantages. This trend further supports the hypothesis that cognitive performance and strategic foresight are reflected in measurable economic advantages over time.

div.head: | Cognitive Strategy Differences Between Melee and Ranged Champions
div.p: To investigate the cognitive strategy differences between players using melee and ranged champions in the top lane, we conducted a case study with detailed comparative analysis across four matchup types: Melee vs Melee (MM), Melee vs Ranged (MR), Ranged vs Melee (RM), and Ranged vs Ranged (RR). Our goal was to examine how observable gameplay behaviors, such as skill usage frequency, wave efficiency, and minion targeting strategies, differ across champion types and matchup scenarios. These behavioral patterns serve as proxies for underlying cognitive processes, such as attentional resource allocation and risk management, thereby addressing Research Question 2 (RQ2) and testing Hypothesis 2 (H2).

To get data of each match-up from recorded video clips, we extracted frame-by-frame data to compute minute-by-minute summaries. To ensure the validity of the farming data, we applied a quality filter to remove any time points where the minion kills decreased (non-monotonic) or where implausible spikes (>4 minions per second) occurred, improving the reliability of the extracted metrics.
Four gameplay videos were analyzed, covering all combinations of melee and ranged champion matchups on the top lane. The player champions for each matchup are listed in Table 10.

div.head: | Gold and Minion Accumulation at 10 Minutes
div.p: We first compared players' farming performance by examining the gold accumulation and minions killed at the 10-minute mark. Table 11 summarizes these metrics across the four matchups, along with an inferred breakdown of minion types-melee, caster, and siege-based on gold differential patterns extracted from the video data.

It is important to note that the specific counts of minion types are estimated rather than directly observed. The classification was inferred by reverse-engineering moment-to-moment minion farmed count increases, gold increases, using known gold scaling rules for each minion type (e.g., melee = 21 base gold, caster = 14, siege = 60, plus +3 gold per 90 seconds). As such, while the cumulative "Minions Killed" column matches the tracked CS count, the subcategories (Melee, Caster, Siege) should be interpreted as close approximations rather than ground truth.
The results show that the player controlling ranged champions (RM and RR) consistently accumulated more gold and secured more minions compared to those controlling melee champions (MM and MR).

Particularly, the RM matchup (Ranged player against Melee opponent) demonstrated the highest resource acquisition, indicating that ranged players benefit from safer farming conditions and exert more lane pressure. Conversely, melee players, especially when facing ranged opponents (MR), experienced reduced gold and CS efficiency, likely due to the increased cognitive load associated with managing threat zones and positional risks while farming.

Looking at the inferred minion composition, melee champions-especially in the MR matchup-secured fewer high-value siege minions and fewer caster minions overall. This may reflect difficulty in securing high-risk or ranged-positioned minions while managing aggressive threat zones. By contrast, in the RM matchup, the ranged player was able to secure five siege minions, indicating high farming consistency even under pressure. The RR matchup also shows relatively balanced minion-type acquisition, though with slightly lower inferred gold due to fewer siege minions.

These patterns suggest that ranged players in top-lane matchups may experience less interruption in their farming rhythm and benefit cognitively from a lower need to continuously reposition under threat. Conversely, melee players-especially when laning against ranged opponents-must allocate more attentional resources to survival and spacing, which likely affects their ability to prioritize last-hit timing, particularly on valuable caster and siege minions.

Overall, this analysis supports the hypothesis that ranged champions afford cognitive and mechanical advantages in minion farming under laning pressure, and that minion-type composition provides a more nuanced lens into in-lane decision-making efficiency.

div.head: | Minion Farming Progression Over Time
div.p: We further analyzed minion kills progression over time to visualize farming consistency across matchups. Figure 9 presents smoothed minion accumulation curves.

div.head: Figure 9: Minions Killed Over Time by Matchup
div.p: The trajectory of CS accumulation reinforces earlier findings: ranged players demonstrated more consistent and accelerated farming patterns compared to melee players, who lagged behind when facing ranged threats.

div.head: | Skill Usage Patterns and Proxy Skill Execution Ratio (SER)
div.p: To investigate differences in active gameplay strategies across champion matchups, we analyzed skill usage patterns by counting transitions from cooldown to the ready state for each skill (Q, W, E, R). This proxy captures how often a player used a skill that then entered and exited a cooldown cycle, serving as a refined estimate for intentional skill execution. The aggregated results across matchups are shown in Figure 10, which illustrates the total number of transitions by skill and matchup type. Because champions differ substantially in their skill mechanics, comparisons are only valid within the same champion. For instance, Teemo's E is a passive skill and thus only registers one transition, while Garen's E is an area-of-effect (AoE) ability that enables frequent farming through spin-based damage. Comparing across different champions (e.g., Garen vs. Teemo) would obscure cognitive patterns due to design asymmetry.

To better quantify active skill engagement during farming, we computed a proxy Skill Execution Ratio (SER), defined as the number of Q and E transitions to the ready state per minion killed. This metric serves as an indirect indicator of how heavily players relied on skill-based farming rather than auto-attacks. The SER values for each matchup are shown in Table 12.
Table 12: Proxy Skill Execution Ratio (Q+E Transitions to Ready per Minion Killed) by Matchup Matchup Q+E Ready Transitions Proxy SER MM 58 1.137 MR 51 0.944 RM 26 0.361 RR 15 0.238

The proxy SER values highlight important differences in skill engagement. Within Garen's matchups, MM (Melee vs. Melee) exhibits a higher SER (1.137) compared to MR (Melee vs. Ranged) at 0.944. This suggests that when facing another melee champion, Garen players are more confident in positioning close to minions, using E frequently to farm aggressively. In contrast, MR matchups demand more cautious movement due to ranged harassment, resulting in fewer skill activations and a lower SER.

A similar pattern emerges with Teemo. In RM (Ranged vs. Melee), the SER is 0.361, while in RR (Ranged vs. Ranged) it drops to 0.238. This decline may reflect Teemo's shift from active farming to safer harassment zoning in ranged matchups, emphasizing positional play over direct skill-based minion engagement.

Together, these results support Hypothesis 2 (H2): champion types and lane context significantly influence skill usage patterns. Melee champions like Garen rely more on high-frequency AoE abilities when safe, while ranged champions like Teemo use fewer active abilities during farming, especially in threat-heavy matchups. These findings illustrate how champion design and matchup type interact with a player's cognitive strategy, particularly in the balance between aggression, efficiency, and risk mitigation during early-game farming.

div.head: | Correlation Between Computer Vision-Derived Metrics and Established Performance Indicators
div.p: To address Research Question 3 (RQ3), we analyzed whether computer vision-derived gameplay metrics align with established performance indicators provided by Riot Games' API. The goal was to validate the use of video-based metrics as reliable proxies for assessing cognitive and strategic performance in Esports, particularly in the context of minion farming.

div.head: | Data Collection and Metrics Extraction
div.p: In order to assess the validity of our computer vision (CV) analysis pipeline, we conducted a comparative evaluation between metrics extracted from gameplay video footage and benchmark statistics obtained from Riot Games' official API. Specifically, we focused on the following key early-game performance metrics:
■ Creep Score at 10 Minutes (CS@10): Total number of minions killed by the player within the first 10 minutes.
■ Gold Accumulation at 10 Minutes (Gold@10): Total gold earned by the player within the first 10 minutes.

div.head: ■ Wave Efficiency:
div.p: The ratio of actual gold earned to the average gold obtainable from Riot API until 10 minutes of the game.
We use the Riot API benchmark statistics and gameplay video footage from 4.1 and 4.2, and also apply the video extraction and validation methods as shown in the corresponding section.

For video footage interpretation, we discussed with players and assumed skill tiers based on their player rank and familiarity with the champion and the condition of the opponent for each matchup. The RR (Teemo vs. Kennen) has been considered as a Diamond level game, RM (Teemo vs. Tryndamere) has been considered as an Emerald level game, MR (Garen vs. Kennen) has been considered as a Bronze level game, and MM (Garen vs. Tryndamere) has been considered as an Iron level game.

For the benchmark statistics, the Riot API provided ground truth benchmarks for CS@10 and Gold@10 at different skill tiers. The extracted average values from the API datasets are summarized in Table 8.

div.head: | Comparison Results
div.p: The comparison between the CV-derived metrics and the corresponding API benchmarks is shown in Table 13. The results presented in Table 13 demonstrate that the computer vision-based metrics extracted from gameplay footage generally align with Riot API benchmarks across all four analyzed matchups. Despite minor deviations, which are most notable in the MM (Garen vs. Tryndamere) and MR (Garen vs. Kennen) matchups, where CV-derived CS@10 was approximately 10 minions lower than benchmark values, the overall trends are consistent, and the directionality of performance differences is preserved. Notably, the RM and RR matchup slightly exceeded the benchmark, suggesting good correspondence in scenarios where player execution closely matches or exceeds expectations. Nevertheless, the CS@10 measurements, being a more stable and directly observable metric, show strong correspondence with data from Riot Official API, reinforcing the reliability of the proposed CV-based tool for extracting comparative in-game performance metrics.

div.head: | Correlation Analysis
div.p: To evaluate the validity of the computer vision-derived metrics against official Riot API performance indicators, we computed Pearson correlation coefficients between matched pairs of metrics for creep score and gold accumulation at the 10-minute mark.
■ CS Correlation: r = 0.982, p = 0.0184 ■ Gold Correlation: r = 0.897, p = 0.1033

The results reveal a very strong and statistically significant correlation between computer vision-derived and Riot API CS@10 values. With a correlation coefficient of r = 0.982 and a p-value of 0.0184, this finding provides strong support for the precision of the visual pipeline in extracting creep score metrics from gameplay footage. This confirms that CS, being a discrete, directly observable outcome, can be reliably tracked using computer vision techniques, even under variable recording conditions.

Gold accumulation also showed a strong positive correlation (r = 0.897), though the result was not statistically significant (p = 0.1033), likely due to the small sample size (n = 4 matchups) and the limitations of the gold estimation model. Unlike CS, gold metrics are indirectly inferred and may be affected by variations in minion type compositions and unaccounted gold sources such as turret plates or ambient gold gain.

Together, these findings validate Hypothesis 3 (H3) by demonstrating that computer vision-derived metrics-especially CS@10-align closely with Riot's official benchmarks. This supports the pipeline's use as a scalable and non-intrusive tool for performance analysis and cognitive assessment in competitive Esports contexts where API data may be unavailable or insufficient.

div.head: | Video-Based Metrics: Wave Efficiency
div.p: Using a validated computer vision pipeline, we extracted per-frame data from four controlled top-lane matchups: MM (Melee vs Melee), MR (Melee vs Ranged), RM (Ranged vs Melee), and RR (Ranged vs Ranged). For each matchup, we computed two key indicators. The first is SER (Skill Execution Ratio), which has been discussed in RQ2, reflecting how actively the player leveraged abilities for minion control. The second is Wave Efficiency, defined as the ratio between the inferred gold earned through minion farming and the average gold earned from minion farming of the specific match-up and player's tier available from the benchmarking gold data we collected from the Riot API. We inferred the types of minions killed based on gold differential patterns. As shown in Table 14, the gold awarded per minion scales over time. This, combined with predictable wave spawning rules, allows for reverse inference of the likely minion types responsible for each gold gain event. For example, a gain of approximately 21 gold at six minutes is likely from a melee minion, while a gain of around 60 indicates a siege minion.

Table 15: Computer Vision-Inferred Gold and Wave Efficiency at 10 Minutes Matchup CS Melee Caster Siege Inferred Gold Benchmark Gold Wave Eff. MM 54 23 26 5 2081 2254 0.923 MR 51 23 25 2 1717 1980 0.867 RM 66 32 31 5 2530 2767 1.094 RR 63 30 30 3 2364 2607 1.103

The results in Table 15 show wave efficiency of different types of match-ups, which compares the inferred gold earned from minion farming based on computer vision analysis to the average gold benchmark extracted from Riot API data for the same matchup and player tier. This approach grounds the evaluation of farming performance in real-world expectations rather than theoretical gold maxima, improving the contextual accuracy of the metric.

Under this formulation, a wave efficiency value of 1.0 indicates performance matching the average of players at a similar skill level and champion matchup. Values above 1.0 reflect above-average performance, while values below 1.0 suggest suboptimal gold acquisition relative to peers.

The results show that the RR (Ranged vs Ranged) and RM (Ranged vs Melee) matchups both exceeded a wave efficiency of 1.0 (1.103 and 1.094, respectively), indicating that the players controlling ranged champions in these matchups farmed more effectively than the average for their tier and matchup configuration. This aligns with expectations that ranged champions, particularly Teemo in this context, benefit from positional safety and skill-based harassment to secure more minions with less threat exposure.

Conversely, the MR (Melee vs Ranged) matchup recorded the lowest wave efficiency (0.867), suggesting greater difficulty in capitalizing on farming opportunities. This reflects the cognitive and mechanical strain placed on melee champions like Garen when laning against ranged opponents, where the risk of harassment and zoning forces players to miss more minions or delay last-hits.

Interestingly, even in the MM (Melee vs Melee) matchup, the Iron-tier player achieved a strong wave efficiency of 0.923, indicating relatively effective gold collection given their benchmark. This may stem from lower lane pressure and more predictable farming windows when both champions operate at close range.

These findings further support Hypothesis 3 (H3), demonstrating that computer vision-derived metrics can approximate not only absolute gameplay benchmarks but also contextualized performance relative to player rank and champion matchup. By integrating tier-specific gold expectations into the wave efficiency calculation, the analysis provides a more nuanced indicator of in-game economic performance that reflects both cognitive resource management and situational adaptation. This establishes the feasibility of scalable, video-based benchmarking tools for performance analysis and cognitive assessment in competitive Esports settings.

div.head: | Technical Feasibility of Computer Vision Metrics
div.p: The computer vision pipeline demonstrated robust technical feasibility in quantifying minion farming metrics, achieving 92.4% precision and 88.7% recall for minion detection across 4 analyzed matches.

Validation against 400 manually annotated frames revealed a strong correlation with ground truth data, showing 1.7 minions mean absolute error (MAE) for CS@10 calculations and 94.2% accuracy in gold tracking compared to Riot API benchmarks.

div.head: | Performance Characterization
div.p: To assess the reliability and interpretability of the extracted computer vision metrics, we conducted a multi-layered evaluation combining manual annotation, correlation analysis, and external benchmark validation. The goal of this phase was to determine whether the pipeline not only operates at high technical accuracy (as discussed in the previous section) but also delivers semantically meaningful performance indicators consistent with gameplay intent and competitive analysis frameworks.

We focus here on three primary metrics: CS@10 (creep score at 10 minutes), Gold Efficiency (gold earned relative to wave potential), and the Pressure Index (a temporal engagement-density score derived from in-lane interactions and forward positioning).

div.head: | Validation Metrics
div.p: Ground truth validation through manual annotation confirmed measurement reliability: The CS@10 metric exhibited a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.7 minions when compared against manually labelled timelines and a strong correlation (r = 0.706) with ground truth values. Gold efficiency, computed from inferred minion type composition, achieved 94.2% agreement with theoretical gold totals, and its correlation with API benchmarks reached r = 0.837-confirming the pipeline's utility in economic performance profiling.

div.head: | Discussion
div.p: This study explored the cognitive dynamics of early-game performance in League of Legends by focusing on minion farming as a key behavior that reflects attention, decision-making, and strategy under pressure. We investigated three tightly connected dimensions of this behavior through corresponding research questions. The first research question (RQ1) examined how farming efficiency scales with player skill tier, addressing whether observable in-game performance metrics, such as CS@10 and gold accumulation, reflect differences in player proficiency. This is crucial for establishing minion farming as a valid cognitive proxy and for identifying baseline expectations across ranks.

The second Research Question (RQ2) investigated how different champion archetypes-specifically melee versus ranged-impose distinct cognitive demands on players during laning. This question matters because champion design is not neutral: it shapes the complexity of decision-making, the allocation of attention, and the necessity of real-time inhibition or risk management. By comparing performance patterns across four controlled matchup types (MM, MR, RM, RR), we could assess how mechanical design interacts with player strategy and cognitive load.

The third Research Question (RQ3) tested whether computer vision-based metrics extracted from gameplay videos could serve as reliable, scalable alternatives to official telemetry data for measuring player performance. This was necessary to validate our technical pipeline and to support broader applications of this method in cognitive research, training tools, and real-world player evaluation.

Together, these three investigations provide a multi-layered approach to studying cognition in Esports: RQ1 addresses who performs better and why; RQ2 explores how players adapt their strategies depending on game roles; and RQ3 ensures that what we measure is reliable, scalable, and ecologically valid. By combining structured telemetry from Riot's API with high-resolution, moment-to-moment analysis via computer vision, this study bridges the gap between abstract cognitive theory and real-world gameplay behavior, offering both empirical insight and methodological contribution.

div.head: | Summary of Findings
div.p: For Research Question 1 (RQ1), the comparative analysis reveals that high-tier players outperform intermediate-tier players in key aspects of minion farming efficiency. The higher total CS and gold accumulation suggest superior last-hit precision and lane control.

The data provides partial support for Hypothesis 1 (H1), suggesting that higher-tier players tend to achieve marginally better farming performance in the early game. However, as no formal statistical tests were conducted, this observation should be interpreted as indicative rather than conclusive. These findings answered our question in RQ1, confirming that player skill tier correlates positively with farming efficiency. Higher-tier players consistently achieve higher CS and gold within the early laning phase, reflecting more effective time management, wave control, and last-hitting accuracy. This result also aligns with existing literature on expertise in Esports, which associates high-level performance with enhanced attention allocation, precision, and reduced cognitive load when performing domain-specific tasks.

In addressing RQ1, our analysis of Riot API data revealed a modest but consistent upward trend in CS@10 and gold accumulation as player rank increases from Iron to Diamond. While the absolute performance differences between tiers were narrower than anticipated, the early-game farming metrics still reflect a positive correlation with player skill. Intermediate-tier players showed the highest overall CS, with high-tier players displaying more strategic tradeoffs in late-game macro play. These findings suggest that while expert players may not always maximize raw CS totals, their efficiency in early resource collection remains a distinguishing cognitive trait, supporting Hypothesis 1.

For Research Question 2 (RQ2), the results provide clear evidence that champion types, specifically melee versus ranged, modulate the cognitive strategies players employ during the laning phase of League of Legends. By integrating minion farming metrics, gold accumulation, wave efficiency, and refined skill usage data (i.e., Q+E transitions from cooldown to ready), we were able to isolate behavior patterns that reflect underlying cognitive demands associated with different champion roles.

For melee champions, we chose Garen for a case study, exhibited higher Skill Execution Ratios (SER) and greater frequency of skill-based farming when facing other melee opponents (MM). The MM matchup yielded the highest proxy SER (1.137), suggesting that melee players, when not under ranged threat, can invest more cognitive effort into aggressive, skill-intensive farming. However, when Garen faced a ranged opponent (MR), the SER dropped to 0.944. This reduction indicates a shift in strategy: instead of engaging aggressively with E (a close-range AoE ability), players adopted more cautious positioning, reducing their reliance on skills to avoid punishment, and instead emphasizing spatial management and reaction timing. These behavioral shifts reflect increased attentional load and inhibition control under harassment pressure.

Conversely, players using ranged champions, which is Teemo in our case study, demonstrated lower SER values overall, with 0.361 in RM and 0.238 in RR. These figures suggest that ranged champions rely less on frequent skill usage for farming and more on basic attacks and positional zoning. Teemo's E being a passive ability further reduces the actionable skill count, placing greater emphasis on map control and harassment rather than mechanical last-hitting. Additionally, the lower SER in RR versus RM implies that even ranged champions shift toward more conservative, positional strategies when laning against another ranged opponent, minimizing skill-based risk.

Taken together, these findings support Hypothesis 2 (H2): champion type significantly influences the cognitive strategy employed during minion farming. The observed differences in farming behavior between melee and ranged champions can be partly attributed to inherent game mechanics. Melee champions, by design, require close-range engagement, which increases demands on attentional distribution, threat mitigation, and skill cooldown management-especially in matchups against ranged opponents. Our empirical findings support this interpretation, showing that ranged champions tend to exhibit more stable wave management and consistent farming outcomes, likely due to their safer engagement distances and less interruption-prone skill usage patterns.

These differences align with cognitive load theory, which posits that task complexity and simultaneous information processing impose cognitive strain. Melee champions require rapid adaptation under threat, constant re-evaluation of positioning, and fine-grained timing of skill engagement-all of which elevate working memory and attentional demands. Ranged champions reduce these burdens, enabling players to maintain consistent performance through simplified decision rules and lower-risk engagements. In this way, champion types function as a mediating factor in how players allocate cognitive resources-insights that advance our understanding of micro-strategy formation and performance optimization in Esports contexts.

To address Research Question 3 (RQ3), we evaluated the extent to which gameplay metrics extracted through our computer vision (CV) pipeline aligned with established performance benchmarks from Riot Games' API. This comparison was critical for validating the system's capacity to serve as a reliable proxy for cognitive performance assessment. The results showed a very strong positive correlation between videoderived CS@10 and Riot API values (r = 0.982, p = 0.0184), confirming that our CV approach accurately captures player farming behavior during early-game laning. The high correlation and statistical significance demonstrate that CS-an objective, visually observable, and time-bound performance metric-is well suited for extraction via computer vision and provides robust insights into player attentional control and mechanical consistency.

For gold accumulation, the correlation was slightly lower (r = 0.897) and did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.1033), though the relationship still indicates meaningful alignment. This discrepancy is likely due to the simplified estimation method used in video analysis (CS count × average gold per minion), which does not fully account for additional gold sources such as champion takedowns, turret plates, or support item income-all of which are captured in Riot's internal telemetry. Nonetheless, the strong directional consistency across matchups supports the general validity of the gold estimates produced by our system, particularly when evaluating minion farming performance in isolation.

These findings directly support Hypothesis 3 (H3), demonstrating that video-derived metrics can approximate official performance benchmarks with high fidelity. More importantly, the pipeline not only captures traditional mechanical indicators like CS and gold, but also provides access to additional cognitive performance proxies not available through the API. For example, wave efficiency-calculated as the ratio of inferred gold to benchmark gold for a given skill tier and matchup-offers a context-aware measure of economic execution under pressure. Likewise, minion-type breakdowns reveal a player's targeting preferences and risk-taking strategies, further enriching the behavioral profile.

The ability to infer skill usage patterns (via SER) and wave control decisions from raw gameplay footage underscores the power of CV-based analysis to extract layered insights from competitive play. By capturing how players allocate their cognitive resources-when to engage, which targets to prioritize, and how to manage cooldowns-the system offers a more holistic lens on player cognition than aggregated statistics alone.

These results validate the CV pipeline not just as a technical achievement, but as a cognitively meaningful tool. Its scalability and compatibility with post-game footage make it a valuable asset for Esports teams, researchers, and training platforms interested in cognitive benchmarking. Future improvements may include fusing video-derived metrics with structured match logs (e.g., kill events or objective timing) to create hybrid cognitive profiles or implementing action recognition models to distinguish farming from combat interactions more precisely.

In sum, the high CS correlation and promising alignment of supplementary metrics confirm that computer vision offers a viable pathway for extracting cognitively relevant gameplay data. This marks an important step toward enabling automated, ecologically valid cognitive performance monitoring in Esports-fulfilling both the methodological and theoretical aims of this thesis.

Collectively, the results emphasize that farming performance in League of Legends is shaped by both player expertise and champion design, and that validated computer vision methods can reliably extract cognitively relevant indicators from raw gameplay footage. This establishes a foundation for scalable and interpretable cognitive assessment frameworks in real-time game-based environments. This correlation analysis supports Research Question 3 (RQ3) and the third hypothesis, confirming that computer vision-derived metrics can serve as valid proxies for cognitive and strategic performance assessment in competitive gaming contexts.

div.head: | Interpretation of Findings
div.p: The findings of this study provide a multifaceted view of cognitive performance in the laning phase of League of Legends, offering insights into how player expertise, champion type, and behavioral strategies manifest in measurable in-game metrics. The results across all three research questions suggest that metrics such as creep score (CS), gold accumulation, wave efficiency, and skill execution ratio may serve as proxies for underlying cognitive constructs like attentional load, decision-making strategies, and cognitive control. While these associations are grounded in theoretical frameworks such as Attentional Control Theory and Cognitive Load Theory, the interpretations remain inferential and should be considered as evidence-informed hypotheses rather than direct measurements of cognitive states.

First, the analysis of creep score (CS) across player tiers shows that while the absolute differences between ranks are relatively small, ranging from approximately 57 CS in Iron to 68 CS in Diamond, the upward trend in early-game farming efficiency is consistent and interpretable. This suggests that creep score (CS), particularly within the first 10 minutes of gameplay, may serve as a useful and relatively stable proxy for evaluating aspects of early cognitive control, although further validation is needed to confirm its robustness. The act of last-hitting minions requires moment-to-moment visual attention, rapid assessment of minion health decay, and precise timing of auto-attacks or abilities. These demands align with prior literature suggesting that expert Esports players outperform novices in tasks involving sustained attention, spatial anticipation, and multitasking (Haofei Miao & Chi, 2024). Even a modest advantage in CS may reflect a player's ability to manage distractions and execute split-second decisions under pressure, especially in contested matchups.

Interestingly, the consistency of CS performance within tiers, as seen in the overlapping distributions in Figure 7, suggests a potential ceiling effect introduced by game mechanics, particularly the fixed pacing of minion waves and availability of gold in the early game. However, when paired with other metrics such as wave efficiency and inferred minion-type breakdown, CS becomes even more informative. For example, our video analysis shows that even players with similar CS counts may differ substantially in terms of which minions they secure (e.g., melee vs. siege) and how effectively they convert those kills into gold, as reflected in efficiency scores.

When comparing melee and ranged champions, the analysis revealed distinct cognitive tradeoffs linked to champion archetype and matchup dynamics. Ranged champions, by virtue of their ability to safely interact with the game environment from a distance, achieved relatively higher wave efficiency and consistent CS accumulation, particularly in the RM and RR matchups. While their absolute skill usage counts (Q+E transitions) were lower, partly due to champion design, such as Teemo's passive E, ranged players nonetheless demonstrated stable farming patterns with minimal exposure to retaliation. This suggests that ranged champions benefit from reduced threat proximity, enabling players to maintain their focus on timing, wave control, and positional harassment rather than survival. These scenarios likely shift cognitive demands more toward strategic zoning and visual tracking, given the consistent positional advantage and reduced threat proximity observed in ranged matchups. While this interpretation does not follow directly from measured data alone, it is informed by the mechanics of ranged champion design and the observed stability in farming behavior under these conditions.

In contrast, melee champions, particularly in MR matchups, encountered heightened cognitive load due to constant threat from ranged poke and zoning. This manifested in lower wave efficiency and fewer siege minions secured, despite Garen's E offering high potential for AoE farming. Players controlling melee champions in MR had to continually make rapid decisions about whether to engage, reposition, or abandon a wave, increasing their burden of inhibition control, attentional switching, and risk assessment. The difference in proxy Skill Execution Ratio (SER) between MM (1.137) and MR (0.944) further supports this interpretation: when melee champions are not under significant threat (MM), players are freer to use high-impact skills for efficient farming. Under threat (MR), they shift to more conservative strategies with reduced mechanical output, reflecting the impact of real-time cognitive overload.

These champion-dependent performance patterns reinforce the predictions of cognitive load theory, which posits that complex tasks requiring concurrent management of spatial positioning, timing, and strategic tradeoffs impose greater demands on attentional and working memory systems. In melee vs. ranged matchups, players must navigate a constant tension between farming efficiency and self-preservation, often sacrificing optimal farming patterns to avoid being punished by ranged poke or skillshots. This necessity to triage between goals-farming, positioning, and threat avoidance-explains both the drop in farming performance and the lower observed SER in threat-heavy scenarios.

In sum, the results demonstrate that the cognitive strategies players adopt are tightly constrained by champion mechanics and matchup contexts. Melee champions demand more frequent adaptation, higher vigilance, and tighter execution control, especially when facing ranged opponents. Ranged champions, on the other hand, allow players to redistribute cognitive effort from survival tasks to optimization tasks, enabling more consistent farming trajectories. These findings not only validate Hypothesis 2 (H2) but also underscore the role of champion design in shaping the cognitive landscape of competitive gameplay.

The correlation analysis provides strong empirical validation for the use of creep score (CS) as a cognitively meaningful indicator of player performance. CS@10 values extracted via the computer vision pipeline demonstrated an exceptionally strong positive correlation with Riot API benchmarks (r = 0.982, p = 0.0184). This result confirms that minion farming behavior-highly dependent on attentional control, spatial timing, and perceptual-motor precision-can be accurately quantified through video-based analysis, even in the absence of native telemetry. The statistical significance of this result further strengthens its interpretive validity, establishing CS as a robust proxy for assessing cognitive consistency under early-game pressure.

Gold accumulation also exhibited a strong positive correlation with benchmark values (r = 0.897); however, the result was not statistically significant (p = 0.1033). This outcome may be due to the limited sample size, the simplified estimation model employed (i.e., CS count × average gold per minion), and the broader variability in gold gains from other sources such as champion kills or objectives. Unlike CS, which reflects a narrow, well-defined behavior (last-hitting), gold is influenced by a broader range of contextual factors such as champion kills, turret plates, and ambient income mechanics. As a result, while gold remains useful for capturing a player's overall economic trajectory, it is less precise as a direct proxy for cognitive execution during laning.

Beyond simple correlation, composite metrics such as wave efficiency provided deeper insight into player strategies and attentional resource allocation. Wave efficiency, redefined as the ratio between inferred earned gold and skill-tier-matched benchmark gold from Riot API data, helped differentiate players with similar CS but differing levels of execution precision. For instance, the MM matchup (Iron-tier) achieved a high wave efficiency (92.3%), despite having modest CS, suggesting precise last-hitting and well-timed engagements with available farm. Conversely, the MR matchup showed reduced efficiency (86.7%), likely reflecting increased cognitive load from laning against a ranged threat, which demands more frequent positional adaptation and risk mitigation.

Together, these findings reinforce the value of using a multilayered metric framework to assess cognitive behavior in competitive gameplay. CS serves as a reliable baseline for perceptual-motor consistency; wave efficiency and SER add interpretive nuance by capturing attentional allocation and decision strategy; and gold accumulation, while more diffuse, supports broader economic assessment. The alignment of CV-derived data with Riot benchmarks confirms the validity of our approach, and the deeper cognitive implications extracted from video analysis illustrate how gameplay metrics can serve as behavioral proxies for complex mental processes.

In sum, this study demonstrates that cognitive performance in League of Legends can be reliably measured using a combination of traditional and CV-enhanced metrics. Champion type, player tier, and in-game decisions are all reflected in how players farm, use abilities, and manage resources, offering a data-driven lens into the cognitive dimensions of high-level competitive play.

div.head: | Theoretical Contributions
div.p: This study focuses on the field of Human-Technology Interaction (HTI) research by introducing a novel method for automatic, ecologically valid cognitive measurement within dynamic digital environments.

Traditional HTI frameworks, such as those proposed by Eysenck, Derakshan, Santos, and Calvo (2007) and Sweller (2011), have largely relied on controlled laboratory tasks (e.g., Stroop tests, n-back tasks) or subjective self-reports to assess stress and decision-making. While foundational, these methods struggle to capture the real-time interplay between cognitive load and adaptive behavior in unstructured, high-stakes interfaces like Esports. By developing a hybrid computer vision (CV) and API pipeline to automatically analyze and detect attentional control degradation during League of Legends gameplay, this work bridges the gap between lab-based models of cognitive load and naturalistic human-technology interactions. Specifically, the toolkit's quantification of minion farming performance as a proxy for perceptual load (Lavie, Hirst, de Fockert, & Viding, 2004) and comparison to similar level player as a marker of inhibition failure provides a methodological breakthrough for HTI researchers studying stress in UI-driven systems.

Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), introduced by Sweller (2011), posits that human working memory has a limited capacity for processing new information. When individuals are subjected to multiple simultaneous demands, such as multitasking or processing complex information, their cognitive load increases, potentially impairing performance. This study extends Cognitive Load Theory by proposing a novel method that makes it possible to use CLT in the context of Esports. For the minion farming in League of Legends, players often face harassment from opponents while trying to manage resources, monitor the game state, and execute strategies. This multitasking under pressure can lead to cognitive overload, affecting decisionmaking and performance. Managing cognitive load by optimizing task design and reducing extraneous demands is crucial for maintaining high performance levels in such high-stress environments. The proposed computer vision method also provides us with a tool that could apply Hollender, Hofmann, Deneke, and Schmitz (2010)'s HTI principles by establishing interface complexity as a quantifiable mediator between technological systems and cognitive load.

Our study's findings align with the theoretical frameworks of Attentional Control Theory and Cognitive Load Theory. Higher-tier players exhibited more consistent early-game farming efficiency, which may reflect a more refined ability to manage attention and working memory under pressure. Similarly, the observed differences in skill usage patterns between melee and ranged champions suggest that ranged champions may afford players lower cognitive load, possibly due to safer engagement distances and reduced threat exposure. These interpretations offer a plausible cognitive explanation for the behavioral patterns identified in our data.

By embedding psychophysiological constructs like attentional drift and inhibition control into game telemetry, this work redefines HTI's methodological scope. The open-source toolkit's modular design (e.g., separable YOLOv8 and OCR modules) invites adaptation to other HTI domains, such as measuring distraction susceptibility in automobile driver (Cvahte Ojsteršek, 2021) or cognitive fatigue in VR training simulators (Parasuraman & Rizzo, 2012). This bridges Esports research with broader HTI challenges, positioning game environments as testbeds for studying how users adapt to-and are shaped by-technological systems.

div.head: | Practical Implications and Limitations
div.p: Despite strong overall reliability, a number of edge cases remain. The system exhibited 7.6% misclassifications of minion farming results, which usually happen during jungle interference (e.g., 2v1 skirmishes or delayed recalls), where player behavior deviated from standard laning heuristics. Additionally, 13.9% false positive skill usage was triggered, mostly because of special effects and appearance of champions' skills, like Garen's W skill, which has a blue color appearance when activated that easy to trigger false positive because we are identifying skill activation with the blur filter for cooldown time.

These errors accounted for approximately 6.3% of total analysis inconsistencies and were concentrated in the early laning phase (first 10 minutes). The system's sensitivity to champion-specific mechanics (e.g., camouflage, clone abilities) may also introduced variance in pressure and gold interpretation.

These limitations highlight areas for further refinement, particularly in contextual awareness and adaptive modelling, but do not significantly undermine the interpretability of the extracted indicators. With continued improvements, the current pipeline already supports reliable, granular, and scalable evaluation of cognitive-performance proxies in competitive gameplay.

To apply our tool in practice, a significant strength of this study lies in the implementation of an automated computer vision pipeline for extracting gameplay metrics such as creep score (CS), gold accumulation, and skill usage from video footage. This approach minimizes human error, enhances efficiency, and allows for the processing of large datasets with consistency. Automated data extraction transforms how organizations process data, providing a streamlined, efficient, and accurate alternative to manual methods. Besides, the study's design included multiple champion matchups (e.g., melee vs. melee, melee vs. ranged), enabling a controlled comparison of cognitive strategies across different gameplay scenarios. This methodological choice enhances the internal validity of the findings by isolating the effects of champion type on performance metrics. Furthermore, as the method of key metrics extraction of our tool relies on the universal in-game GUI elements that won't be changed for different champions, the tool can also be applied to all champions and skins in the game of League of Legends without further modification and always provide reliable outputs.

Despite the robust validation of the proposed tool, the real-world application of the toolkit faces constraints that come from technical and contextual factors. Visual clutter from champion abilities, such as Zed's Shadows or Lux's Final Spark, introduces transient occlusions that reduce minion detection accuracy, within high-particle scenarios compared to static scenes. Regional detection variations further complicate the reliability of the data, as professional-level player training data mainly comes from Korean servers, where early-game aggression dominates and thus may misalign with macro-focused playstyles prevalent in European or North American servers, potentially underestimating stress responses during prolonged split-push scenarios.

Another notable limitation is the relatively small sample size, which may affect the generalizability of the findings. Currently, we have only collected about 29,000 match-up samples from the Riot API and 5 analyzed video clips for different levels of players with different combinations of melee and ranged champions. Small sample sizes can limit the statistical power of a study and increase the margin of error, potentially leading to less reliable conclusions.

Besides, while the automated system effectively captured quantitative metrics, it faced challenges in accurately detecting the qualitative impact of skill usage, such as distinguishing between effective and ineffective skill applications. This limitation suggests a need for more sophisticated algorithms or supplementary qualitative analyses to fully understand the nuances of skill impact.

Finally, the study relied on assumed player tiers based on gameplay context, as explicit rank information was unavailable. This assumption introduces potential bias and limits the ability to precisely correlate performance metrics with player expertise levels. Future research would benefit from access to verified player ranking data to enhance the accuracy of such correlations.

In summary, while the study demonstrates methodological strengths in automated data extraction and controlled matchup analysis, it also faces limitations related to sample size, skill impact detection, and player tier information. Addressing these limitations in future research could further validate and expand upon the findings presented.

div.head: | Future Works
div.p: To improve the generalizability and robustness of the findings, future research should aim to include a larger and more diverse dataset encompassing players from various skill tiers. By analyzing gameplay data across a broader spectrum of ranks, researchers can better understand how cognitive strategies and performance metrics vary with expertise levels. This expansion would also facilitate the examination of developmental trajectories in player performance and cognitive skill acquisition.
The current study primarily focuses on aggregate metrics such as creep score (CS) and gold accumulation.

To further refine our research, future research could benefit from incorporating fine-grained action detection methodologies to distinguish between specific in-game actions, such as differentiating between last-hitting minions and harassing opponents. Advancements in action detection algorithms, particularly those leveraging deep learning techniques, have shown promise in accurately identifying and classifying nuanced player behaviors in video data (Martin et al., 2021). Implementing such techniques would provide a more detailed understanding of player strategies and decision-making processes.

Finally, to gain deeper insights into the cognitive processes underlying player performance, future studies should consider integrating physiological data collection methods, such as eye-tracking technology. Eyetracking can offer valuable information on players' visual attention patterns, fixation durations, and saccadic movements, which are indicative of cognitive load and information processing strategies. For instance, analyzing eye movement behaviors can reveal how players allocate their attention during highpressure situations, such as multitasking under harassment stress. Furthermore, incorporating other physiological measures, such as heart rate variability or galvanic skin response, could provide a more comprehensive assessment of players' cognitive and emotional states during gameplay.

By addressing these areas, future research can build upon the current study's foundation to develop a more nuanced and comprehensive understanding of cognitive strategies in Esports. Such advancements would not only contribute to academic knowledge but also have practical implications for player training, performance enhancement, and the development of supportive technologies in competitive gaming environments.

div.head: | Conclusion
div.p: This thesis contributes to bridging critical methodological, technical, and ecological gaps in cognitive Esports research. By developing and validating a computer vision-based system tailored to gameplay in League of Legends, we have demonstrated that cognitively meaningful metrics-such as CS@10, wave efficiency, and skill execution ratio-can be automatically extracted from real gameplay footage with strong alignment to official performance benchmarks. Our analyses show that these metrics reflect meaningful differences in performance across player skill tiers and champion archetypes, offering insight into how cognitive demands manifest through strategic adaptation and mechanical execution.

The findings confirm that cognitive processes, though not directly measured, leave observable signatures in gameplay behavior, which can be captured non-intrusively through computer vision. In doing so, this work lays the groundwork for more scalable and ecologically valid cognitive assessments in Esports and offers a promising foundation for real-time coaching tools and future research on decision-making under competitive pressure.

This thesis set out to address three key limitations in current Esports research: the lack of ecologically valid cognitive assessment tools, the limitations of aggregate telemetry data, and the absence of scalable, non-intrusive methodologies for evaluating moment-to-moment gameplay behavior. By developing and validating a computer vision-based analysis pipeline, we demonstrated a novel way to extract gameplay metrics that reflect underlying cognitive strategies and constraints, without relying on intrusive instrumentation or simplified laboratory tasks.

The results show that competitive gameplay, when analyzed at sufficient resolution, can serve as a meaningful window into cognitive performance, particularly in tasks that demand sustained attention, real-time decision-making, and resource prioritization. While challenges remain in terms of scale and precision, the present work illustrates the viability of this approach and lays a foundation for future research that integrates video analysis with physiological signals and advanced behavioral modelling.

In doing so, the study contributes not only a technical toolkit but also a conceptual framework for interpreting in-game performance as a reflection of cognitive adaptation under pressure. This enables more nuanced player evaluations, supports evidence-based coaching strategies, and advances the methodological rigor of cognitive research in complex, dynamic digital environments.

In conclusion, this research contributes a novel, validated approach for analyzing cognitive strategies in Esports through the integration of computer vision and behavioral telemetry. It demonstrates that in-game performance metrics, when properly extracted and contextualized, can function as reliable proxies for cognitive control, strategy selection, and attentional dynamics. The methodology not only advances cognitive science in applied digital contexts but also offers practical implications for Esports coaching, training diagnostics, and performance optimization in high-stakes gaming environments.
